title: Strength restoration strategies
summary: NH explains 'strength restoration': light, non-invasive tendon-focused exercises, mostly with bands, supersetted inside every workout to nurse old injuries and prevent re-aggravation. He describes his six routines (S1-S3, R1-R3), how they double as nucleus overload for lagging muscles, and why they must never be scheduled outside training.
claims: Strength restoration means small non-invasive resistance exercises in specific reps and angles that target tendons of problem areas, with almost no recovery cost; a kind of active stretching, not a warm-up
Healed injuries can linger as tendon damage, often aggravated tendinitis; signs are feeling it after poor sleep, on waking or in the cold
Never schedule rehab work outside training: you will skip it, and even skipping once every three days compounds over a year
Strength restoration must be supersetted between sets of the main lifts; unlike real strength work it is non-invasive, warms the area and makes the lift less painful
I run six routines, three S and three R; at least two happen every day, up to four, never more than four
My catalogue: S1 calves, S2 neck, S3 shoulders, R1 ribs and lats, R2 triceps, R3 ribs
I broke ribs twice and tore intercostals squatting, so I do my rib routine between warm-up and top sets of squats and deadlifts, which aggravate them
Reps barely matter for strength restoration, roughly 10-15, and two movements per routine on different planes is enough; three was overkill
Strength restoration is essentially nucleus overload applied to tendons; it can also be used as nucleus overload for a lagging muscle
When used as nucleus overload, avoid placing it on days that tire that muscle: my triceps routine never goes on bench day and my calf routine not on heavy squat/deadlift days
Stimulating the tendon stimulates the muscle and vice versa; nucleus-overload triceps work also helps elbow health
Bands are the best tool for tendon work; I use a dumbbell for lat pullovers to stretch the ribcage and plates for calves and neck
Isolating my neck cured the neck pain I used to get from presses; training calves reduces ankle and foot pain
Strength restoration can cure minor tendinitis and is the best way to hammer lagging muscles that you would otherwise skip at the end of workouts
Start with one routine for your worst area and build up; I began with one for my ribs and am now capped at six
